new:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{A mechanistic account of what off-path staging does in the
  shipped driver.} A stager that makes pages resident cannot prevent faults,
  because only fault service maps a page (verified from source and by
  counters). Its gain against the shipped driver comes through the
  prefetcher's density rule, which counts staged pages as resident, confirmed
  by a pre-registered dose--response test; about 86\% of the drop in dispatch
  time is fewer faults rather than cheaper ones. At matched thresholds it adds
  at most 2.8\%. Copy offload is large only when the prefetcher is off.

  \item \textbf{New measurements of the prefetch threshold.} On system-allocated
  (HMM) memory, a low threshold slows sparse access by up to 204\% with the
  array in GPU memory, where managed memory shows only a few percent. With
  access density isolated by a synthetic benchmark and migrated bytes traced, the
  density rule reproduces the measured volume exactly. These measurements also
  replicate, on two newer GPU generations and a newer driver, both directions
  of the trade-off that Go \emph{et al.}\ reported.

  \item \textbf{An in-driver off-path staging prototype with a first-touch
  oracle.} A modification of NVIDIA's open-source UVM driver with a fast,
  lock-free oracle and a configurable staging width, and the measured cost of
  each part on the critical path (54--75\,ns per enqueue on the stencil
  workload). Its kernel changes passed a review protocol of compile-only review,
  a precondition table for every driver call, and an attended first load.

  \item \textbf{A falsifiable measurement protocol, exercised.} Every gate fixed
  its families, statistic, test, minimum detectable effect, and falsification
  trigger in a committed file before running. Three triggers fired, and each
  changed the paper's conclusion. Analysis uses medians, two-sided
  Mann--Whitney $U$, Holm correction across pre-declared families, bootstrap
  confidence intervals for the null results we rely on, and reports outliers
  with and without removal.

  \item \textbf{A catalog of UVM measurement artifacts.} Thirty-one artifacts
  met in this study, each with the false conclusion it would have produced,
  including the misaligned oracle. One pattern stands out, descriptively: of
  nine errors arising from a mismatch of aggregation level (per batch versus per
  fault, per trial versus per run), eight were caught only by a later,
  independent pass. In all, eleven of the 31 were caught inside the gate that
  made them, three by a check written before the measurement.
\end{itemize}

A non-significant comparison whose
MDE is smaller than an effect of interest is evidence that the effect is
absent at that size. A comparison whose MDE is larger is not evidence
either way.
new:
Eq.~(\ref{eq:mde}) uses standard deviations, so a single slow run
can inflate it far beyond what the rank test sees; on the T4, one cold
SGEMM run raised its MDE from about 0.2\% to 7.7\%. Where we rely on a null
result we therefore argue from a 95\% bootstrap confidence interval of the
difference of medians, with 10{,}000 resamples within cells, as a
percentage of the baseline median. A null whose interval excludes an effect
of interest is evidence that the effect is absent at that size; a wide
interval is not evidence either way. Of the 84 comparisons in this paper,
the interval and the Holm decision disagree in two, both borderline: one interval end lies
within 0.15 percentage points of zero.
